documents: Blanck et al. 2022, J. Volcanol. Geotherm. Res. 431, 107666 (published PDF, 10 pages)
Publisher XML converted to located text (jats_text): abstract and figure captions only
pages_convention: XML section and paragraph locators (jats_text) for the abstract and figure captions. The XML holds no body text, so body-text steps cite printed journal pages, which equal PDF pages counted from 1.

entry.evidence: a small intrusion has been proposed as its cause. In this paper, we study fault activation around the uplift center

sequences.source_document: Blanck et al. 2022, published PDF and XML text

steps.action: Cite the inflating Mogi point source located from GPS, levelling and InSAR by Sigmundsson et al. (1997) and Feigl et al. (2000).
steps.quote: Feigl et al. (2000) confirmed and refined those findings

steps.action: Cite the rival causes of the uplift: a small magmatic intrusion (Feigl et al.) or a hydrothermal origin (Tryggvason et al.).
steps.quote: The cause of the uplift remains unresolved, a small magmatic intrusion has been suggested

steps.action: Cite Feigl et al.'s earlier Coulomb comparison, which put most catalogue hypocentres in regions of increased Coulomb stress.
steps.quote: found that most of the earthquake hyopocentres are located in parts of the crust where the Coulomb stress increases

steps.action: Compare the Hengill uplift with other Icelandic intrusions, note its unusual amount of seismicity, and pose the question this raises.
steps.quote: raising the question how a relatively small uplift could have such extensive consequences

steps.action: Design the test: map faults near the uplift that were likely triggered directly, then model the source's Coulomb stress change on them; select the study box around the uplift.
steps.quote: [...] this study is to analyze the seismic activity in the direct vicinity of the uplift

steps.action: Use SIL network catalogue data and stored waveforms for 1993-1998, with manually revised picks and polarities; over 12,000 events lie in the study area.
steps.quote: We use catalogue data and waveforms from the SIL network from Jan 1st 1993 to Dec 31st 1998

steps.action: Observe that the catalogue hypocentres are diffuse, without visible faults, and that routine locations have errors of 500-700 m horizontally and about 1000 m in depth.
steps.quote: linear alignments or clear faults are not obvious to the naked eye

steps.action: Relocate the events with Slunga double-difference relocation, using cross-correlation (CC at least 0.8), the SUL velocity model and groups of 9-45 events; 10,406 events are relocated.
steps.quote: The locations of a subset of 12,000 micro-earthquakes are significantly improved by a double-difference relocation algorithm

steps.action: Identify 25 faults from the relocated seismicity with QuakeLook best-fitting planes; most of the seismicity stays scattered.
steps.quote: twenty-five (25) rectangular prisms, consisting of 11 to 363 earthquakes and 200 to 3000 m long, were identified and are interpreted as faults

steps.action: Estimate double-couple focal mechanisms from first motions plus spectral amplitudes, pick the nodal plane closest to each fault plane, and compute average and magnitude-weighted slip vectors; most faults are near-vertical and right-lateral strike-slip.
steps.quote: Focal mechanism analysis of individual events was applied to estimate slip direction on these faults.

steps.action: Vary the relocation group size and group spacing over 7 parameter sets to estimate location uncertainty (about 260 m horizontal, 800 m depth standard deviation).
steps.quote: we test different input parameters in the relocation process

steps.action: Compare the faults mapped at depth with the independently mapped surface faults of Clifton et al. (2002) and Steigerwald et al. (2018).
steps.quote: there is a reassuring concordance between the strike of our faults and the mapped surface faults

steps.action: Synthesize cited intrusion-seismicity studies (Pedersen et al., Rubin and Gillard, Keiding et al.) into the hypothesis that the Hengill crust was near failure and the uplift acted as a trigger.
steps.quote: this implies that the region was near-failure prior to the uplift

steps.action: Compute with Coulomb 3 the Coulomb stress change from Feigl et al.'s inflation source on the 25 mapped receiver faults (Poisson ratio 0.25, friction 0.4, Young's modulus 80 GPa).
steps.quote: We calculated the Coulomb stress change (CSC) caused by the inflation at the location and with volume change proposed by Feigl et al.

steps.action: Compare the computed stress change with the observed slip: positive on 18 faults, none on 4, negative on 3 with average rake; 17, 3 and 5 with weighted rake.
steps.quote: We found a marked increase on 18 of the 25 mapped faults

steps.action: Recompute the stress change with the source moved 1 km north and 1 km south, within Feigl et al.'s error margins, for both rake averages.
steps.quote: We re-calculated the CSC on the faults assuming an inflation source both 1 km further north and south.

steps.action: Refine the source location: a source 1 km further north than Feigl et al.'s appears slightly more plausible.
steps.quote: moving the center of uplift 1 km further north compared to the modeled value from Feigl et al. (2000) appears more plausible

steps.action: Attribute the faults that the stress change would not have triggered to uncertain fault parameters, chiefly rake, rather than rejecting the triggering hypothesis.
steps.quote: the most likely explanation for the discrepancy between the observations and the modelling results

steps.action: Keep the claim that the induced Coulomb stress change could have caused the observed slip on 22 of 25 faults.
steps.quote: the stress changes would have been able to induce the observed fault movement on 22 of 25 faults

steps.action: Keep the sub-claim that near-vertical strike-slip faulting shows a local stress regime dominated by the SISZ transform rather than by rifting.
steps.quote: the stress regime in the study area is dominated by the SISZ transform zone rather than the rifting

tree.answer: 1993-1998 Hengill uplift with an unusually large amount of seismicity
No; faults and slip are inferred from relocated hypocentres and focal mechanisms
Test whether intrusion-induced Coulomb stress change promoted the observed fault slip
Magmatic and hydrothermal origins are named, but only the inflation-source stress change is modelled
No distinct predictions are computed for the rivals
Conditions found: a natural unrest episode recorded by the SIL network

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: One event; repetition only across the 25 receiver faults within it
Largely; source location and rake weighting varied, positive stress change on most faults
Kept: stress change consistent with slip on most faults; mismatches assigned to rake uncertainty

end.claim: The Coulomb stress change from the modelled inflation source, within its location error margins, accounts for the observed slip on most (22 of 25) mapped faults, so the seismicity reflects induced stress acting on a pre-stressed crust.

decisive_move.sentence: Without relocating the events and mapping 25 faults with focal-mechanism rakes, there would be no receiver faults on which to test the induced stress change.

gates.evidence: Action: the data are routine SIL monitoring records; the hypothesis only directed the choice of study area and the analysis (p. 3). Claim: the stress change could have come out negative on most faults, but no failure threshold was set, and the mismatching faults were attributed to rake uncertainty (p. 8). Registration: no analysis plan or threshold was fixed before the data.

imports.item: waveform cross-correlation to refine differential arrival times
weighted least-squares inversion for relative locations

limits: The XML text holds only the abstract and figure captions, so body-text steps cite printed pages and quotes come from the PDF text. The supplement (Table A1, Figs. A1-A9) was not supplied; relocation changes and per-fault details could not be checked. The abstract's 22 of 25 apparently counts the 4 faults with no stress change as consistent (inference from p. 8). The magmatic-versus-hydrothermal rival is named but never given a distinct prediction; only an inflation point source is modelled, so best_explanation rather than confirmed. Composition trace_series fits loosely: one found event, with the 25 faults acting as repeated receivers. The near-failure pre-stress hypothesis (p. 7) is argued from cited studies, not tested. Sub-claims: relocated locations have small internal uncertainty (capability_characterized, p. 9); the SISZ-dominated stress regime (best_explanation, p. 9). No review file was supplied, although the acknowledgements mention two anonymous reviewers.

disagreements.target: Foulger (1988b) and Miller et al. (1998) groupings of Hengill seismicity
disagreements.support: Those studies sampled periods without inflation, deflation or large sequences, so their grouping may not hold during unrest.
disagreements.quote: hence the long-term applicability of seismicity grouping may be questioned

disagreements.target: Feigl et al. (2000) uplift source location
disagreements.support: Stress changes recomputed with the source shifted 1 km north fit slightly more faults with weighted rake, though the difference is minor.
disagreements.quote: moving the center of uplift 1 km further north compared to the modeled value from Feigl et al. (2000) appears more plausible
